newsitem.title: USA: Erickson to leave TWA after turbulent reign.
newsitem.headline: Erickson to leave TWA after turbulent reign.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc chief executive officer Jeffrey Erickson said on Thursday he would leave the company in January, ending a 2-1/2 year reign that included TWA's bankruptcy reorganization and coping with the aftermath of a fatal crash in July.
"I have decided that it is time for me to move on," Erickson, 51, said in a statement released by TWA.
"I look forward to working with the board during the next three months to select a qualified successor and effect a smooth transition," he added.
No further details were given about why Erickson had decided to leave the airline and he was not available for comment.

Earlier on Thursday, TWA reported a third quarter loss of $14.3 million, saying its yield in the quarter suffered, in part due to the loss of premium fare bookings following the crash of TWA Flight 800 on July 17. All 230 people on board perished in the crash.
Erickson's departure comes just four months after chief financial officer Robert Peiser left TWA. At the time, the airline said Peiser quit over differences in management direction.
However, the company distanced Peiser's decision from Erickson's planned resignation. "The two issues are not linked," spokesman John McDonald said.

Some staff were angered by Erickson's decision. "We went through about a CEO a year for a while there," said one pilot. "When he was first coming on board, they had a road show and he was asked, well, how long are you here. He said something along the lines that he was there for the duration."
Erickson joined TWA in April 1994, and was named chief executive officer in August of that year, taking over from Donald Craib Jr., who served less than a year in the post.
His resignation comes as the company is still recovering from the aftermath of the July 17. The cause of the crash has still not been established.
In announcing third quarter results on Thursday, the company said some revenue was lost as a result of the July crash and an extremely aggressive growth plan for summer flying.
Analysts have said the company had significant problems in summer scheduling due, in part, to a delayed delivery of some aircraft that were being refurbished.
The airline recently began taking delivery of its first aircraft ordered under Erickson's reign, which was seen as a positive sign the carrier was recovering after emerging from bankruptcy last year.
